title: Bowen v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
disposition_detail: The SJC sustained Bowen’s complaint against Presbytery’s 1990 rescission of its 1988 ruling and annulment of the officers’ elections, ordinations, and installations. It also held Presbytery’s suspension of a local ruling elder improper without due process. It nevertheless affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals of the system of doctrine for which church officers may receive no exception. The officers remained in office; voluntary demission or proper disciplinary process was advised rather than ordered.
first_summary: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint because ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was impermissible after implementation. It nevertheless affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no exception for church officers. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord, and voluntary demission or proper process was advised.
summary: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

sources.supports: Operative judgment, reasons, officers’ continuing status, doctrinal ruling, and advised next steps.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: The caption identifies SJC Case 90-8, Bowen v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery (lines 16–20); the judgment appears at lines 88–95, with voting at lines 326–328.
evidence_notes.dispute: Presbytery rescinded its 1988 action and annulled officers’ elections and ordinations in 1990; Bowen complained that this occurred without trial (lines 64–68, 78–86; printed pp. 539–540).
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: The complaint was sustained while the doctrinal judgment was affirmed (lines 88–105). Ordination was perpetual, deposition required process, rescission was untimely, and suspension required due process (lines 127–174; printed pp. 542–543).
evidence_notes.qualifications: The officers remained in office despite doctrinal incompatibility; resignation, process, pastoral measures, original jurisdiction, or dissolution were advisory possibilities, not ordered relief (lines 97–121). Two concurring opinions followed; no dissent appears (lines 326–416).
evidence_notes.incorporated_decisions: The SJC adopted applicable principles from Chappel v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery, Case 90-4, concerning censure without due process; those principles and their application here are stated at lines 172–174, though the full incorporated opinion is not supplied.

source_limits: The source includes the adopted judgment, reasoning, concurrences, and Bowen’s later-appended brief. The brief beginning at line 420 is party argument, not adopted reasoning. The full Chappel opinion is absent, but the incorporated principle material here is expressly stated.

score_reasons.concrete_dispute: Identifies the retroactive rescission, annulment, and absence of trial.
score_reasons.decision: States both the sustained procedural complaint and affirmed doctrinal ruling.
score_reasons.decisive_reason: Gives the perpetual-ordination, due-process, and parliamentary grounds.
score_reasons.distinctive_value: Preserves the distinction between doctrinal ineligibility and removal only through proper process.
score_reasons.fidelity: Separates the adopted judgment and advice from concurrences and the appended party brief.
score_reasons.economy: Retains only facts needed to explain the mixed outcome and practical consequence.

verification_notes: Rechecked the operative judgment and reasons at lines 88–174. The final summary adds the separate due-process defect in Presbytery’s suspension, clarifies that the doctrinal issue was affirmed against Bowen, and describes resignation or process as advice rather than mandatory relief.
repair_notes: The catalog header says “Dissent: yes,” but the source records two concurring opinions and no dissent; all participating members concurred, with one member abstaining because he was serving abroad (lines 326–328).
